payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
The strongest objection to provenance is one sentence long. Anyone can sign a false claim. The objection is correct, and answering it badly has cost the field more than the objection ever did.

What the signature binds

A signature attaches a statement to a key at a moment. Verification confirms that whoever held that key committed to that statement then, and that nothing has been altered since.

The operation does not inspect the statement. A producer who signs a record saying they played the bass part produces a perfectly valid signature whether or not they ever touched the instrument. Mathematics has no opinion about session work. It never did, and no amount of key length changes that.

So the claim does not become true by being signed. It becomes fixed and attributed. Those are different properties, and the habit of selling the second while implying the first is why serious people arrive at this work already suspicious of it.

Assertion and observation

Signed claims do not all carry the same weight, and the difference sits in how the record was produced rather than in how it was signed.

A record generated by an instrumented environment reports what that environment observed while the work happened. A record typed in afterward reports what someone remembers, or what they would prefer believed. Both can be signed. Both verify identically. Only one of them was ever in contact with the event it describes.

This is the distinction that the capture argument rests on, and it is worth separating from the cryptography rather than bundling with it. Signing at the source narrows the space where a claim can be false, because the system is recording rather than accepting testimony. Signing a submitted form does not narrow anything. It fixes the testimony in place and names who gave it.

A verification result that returns the same green for both is reporting less than it appears to. The signature is doing its job correctly. The reader is asking it a question nobody asked it to answer.

A false claim with a name on it

The objection assumes that a claim capable of being false is not worth signing. That does not follow, and the reason is visible in how music metadata already fails.

An unsigned false claim has no author. It enters registries and royalty systems with nothing attached to it, gets copied downstream, and the cost of correcting it falls on whoever has the least capacity to chase it. Nobody can be asked about it because there is no one to ask.

A signed false claim has a name and a date. It can be set against an earlier record that contradicts it. The party who made it can be confronted with it, and any consequence that follows is available only because the claim stopped being anonymous. Attribution is what converts a data problem into a conduct problem, and conduct problems have remedies.

That is a smaller promise than the one usually made on provenance's behalf. It is also the one that holds up when money is on the table and somebody's lawyer is reading.

What remains unsolved is not truth. It is legibility: a reader looking at a verified record cannot tell whether they are holding an observation or a well-formed assertion, and nothing in current practice marks the difference.
payload.title: Provenance signs the claim, not the truth
